turns.response_html:
Based on the photo, those are GE Universal T8/T12 LED tubes. Converting these to run on a battery is a bit more complex than just "hooking up some wires," because these bulbs are designed to mimic high-voltage fluorescent tubes.

Here is the breakdown of why this is a challenging DIY project:

The Voltage Gap

  • The Design: These bulbs are "Universal," meaning they are built to work either with an existing fluorescent ballast (which kicks out high voltage) or by being "ballast-bypassed" to run directly on 120V AC (standard wall power).
  • The Internal Driver: Inside that plastic tube is a driver circuit that expects high-voltage alternating current. Most common batteries (like a 12V car battery or a 5V USB pack) provide low-voltage direct current (DC).
  • The Conflict: The internal driver won't "turn on" with a standard battery. To make it work, you would have to use an inverter to turn your battery power into 120V AC, which is inefficient for a DIY lighting project.

Can you "Hack" it?

Technically, yes, but it’s risky.

  1. Opening the Tube: You would have to crack open the sealed tube to bypass the internal GE driver and wire directly to the LED strips inside.
  2. Voltage Matching: You would need to measure the voltage requirements of the bare LED chips. Most internal strips in these tubes operate at a much higher voltage (often 30V–100V DC) than a standard battery provides.

Recommendation

If you want a battery-powered light for a DIY project, it is significantly safer, cheaper, and easier to:

  • Buy 12V LED strips: These are designed to run directly off a battery (like a 12V power tool battery or a car battery) without any dangerous high-voltage conversion.
  • Use the GE bulbs for their intended purpose: Keep them for shop lights or garage fixtures that plug into the wall.

Safety Warning: Never attempt to plug a battery directly into the pins of these bulbs. It won't work, and if you later try to plug a "modified" bulb into a wall outlet, it could result in an electrical fire or explosion.

turns.prompt_text: I have a few of these 6 inch lights these are what I mean not the LEDs Attached 1 file. - e19b81a8-0dc1-4a45-ac2e-1deb99eb384e
turns.response_html:
Actually, these are even trickier than the LED ones! These are fluorescent tubes, which means they don't have any internal electronics to manage power—they rely entirely on an external ballast to work.

Why batteries won't work directly

  • The Science: Fluorescent lights work by sending a high-voltage electric discharge through gas. To start the light, you need a massive "kick" of voltage (often over 300V), and then a steady, regulated current to keep it glowing.
  • The Battery Problem: A battery provides low-voltage DC. If you connect these bulbs directly to a battery, literally nothing will happen—the gas inside won't even begin to glow.

The DIY Reality

To use these with a battery for a project, you would need a DC-to-AC Fluorescent Inverter Ballast. These are small circuit boards specifically designed to take 12V DC and ramp it up to the high-frequency AC these tubes require.

Since you've been working with electronics components like Raspberry Pi Picos and soldering tools, you definitely have the skills to wire one of these up. However, there are some significant downsides to consider for a DIY build:

  • Efficiency: Fluorescents are far less efficient than LEDs when running on battery power; you'll drain your battery much faster.
  • Fragility: Unlike the plastic-encased LEDs you looked at before, these are thin glass tubes filled with a tiny amount of mercury vapor. They are very easy to break during a DIY build.
  • Heat: These tubes get much hotter than LEDs, which can be a problem if you're building them into a small enclosure or using them for a portable project.

Better Alternatives for Your Projects

Given your interest in automatons and DIY electronics, you might find these options more satisfying:

  • CCFL Tubes: If you really love the "neon" look of these tubes, look for Cold Cathode (CCFL) kits. They are similar but often come with the 12V inverters included.
  • LED Filaments: You can buy "flexible LED filaments" that look like the glowing gas in these tubes but run safely on 3V or 12V DC.
